title: The lesson I learned from Jethro advising Moses is a lesson many faithful people learn too late.
paragraphs: The lesson I learned from Jethro advising Moses is a lesson many faithful people learn too late.
Being called by God does not mean carrying everything alone.

When we read Exodus 18, Moses is doing something that looks honorable. From morning until evening, he is standing before the people, listening to disputes, settling arguments, and helping them understand God's laws.

Everyone needs him.
Everyone depends on him.
Everyone comes to him.
At first glance, it looks like dedication.
But when Jethro watched what was happening, he saw something Moses could not see.
Exhaustion.
Pressure.
A system that was slowly breaking the man God had chosen to lead.
And then Jethro said something simple, but incredibly bold:

“What you are doing is not good.”
— Exodus 18:17
That statement is shocking when you think about it.

Moses was not sinning.
He was not rebelling.
He was not avoiding responsibility.
He was serving.
But he was serving in an unsustainable way.
And that is a lesson many believers miss today.
Sometimes the greatest danger in ministry, leadership, family responsibility, or service to others is not disobedience.
It is carrying more than wisdom allows.

Moses believed he had to be available for everything.
Every question.
Every conflict.
Every decision.
But Jethro saw the future if nothing changed.
“You will surely wear yourselves out,” he warned.
Not just Moses.
The people too.
Because when one person becomes responsible for everything, eventually the system collapses under the weight.
Jethro’s solution was not to make Moses work harder.
It was to make Moses work wiser.

He told him to appoint capable leaders.
To divide responsibility.
To build structure.
To focus on the assignments only Moses was meant to carry.
In other words:
Delegation is not weakness. It is wisdom.
But many people struggle with this.
Some believe asking for help means failure.
Some believe stepping back means they are becoming lazy.
Some believe if they do not carry everything, nothing will get done.
But the truth is this:
Even Moses needed wise counsel.
And that may be one of the most powerful lessons in the story.

Moses was powerful.
Chosen by God.
Used to confront Pharaoh.
The man through whom God parted the Red Sea.
Yet even he needed someone to step into his life and say:
“This way is not good.”
Humility allowed Moses to listen.
He did not argue.
He did not defend his exhaustion.
He adjusted.
And because he listened, the entire nation benefited.
Sometimes the reason we are overwhelmed is not because God asked too much of us.
It is because we have taken on responsibilities that wisdom would have distributed.

Burnout is not always rebellion.
Sometimes it is bad structure.
Some people reading this right now are exhausted.

You are trying to solve every problem.
Carry every burden.
Be strong for everyone.
But wisdom may be asking you a difficult question today:
Are you carrying something that was never meant to be carried alone?
Because calling does not cancel human limits.

Even the strongest leaders need help.
Even the most faithful servants need support.
Even the most anointed people need wise voices in their lives.
The lesson from Jethro is simple, but powerful:
Not everything you can carry, you were meant to carry.
Sometimes wisdom does not tell you to pick up more.
Sometimes wisdom tells you to put something down.
And when you do, it does not weaken the mission.
It strengthens it.
Because God never designed His work to crush His servants.
He designed it to be carried with wisdom, humility, and shared responsibility.
So maybe the real question today is this:
What are you still holding that wisdom has already told you to release?
If this message spoke to you, take a moment to reflect and share.
Have you ever experienced burnout because you were carrying too much alone?
